structure.overview: Mr. Shah and his family seek judicial review of a 2019 refusal of their second humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) permanent residence application in Canada, primarily concerning the adequacy of autism services for their son in Bangladesh. The Immigration Officer found that the family was typically established and that autism services were available in Bangladesh, leading to refusal of the exemption. The Federal Court upheld the reasonableness of the decision and dismissed the judicial review application.

sections.label: Tribunal below's decisions on H&C applications
Analysis of establishment and application of legal test
Analysis of autism services and best interests of the child

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah, his wife, and son with ASD from Bangladesh seek judicial review of a 2019 refusal of his second H&C permanent residence application.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah's education and work history in Bangladesh and UK, refugee claim in Canada rejected in 2015 for lack of fear and anti-government blogger status.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: In 2015, their son was diagnosed with moderate to severe ASD and receives behavioural services and an individual education plan in Toronto.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: First H&C application in 2017 refused due to insufficient hardship evidence and available autism services in Bangladesh; return not against children's best interests.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: 2018 judicial review dismissed; officer's procedural fairness and assessment of children's best interests upheld.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Pre-removal risk assessment application also refused in September 2017.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Second H&C application in 2018 reviewed; Immigration Officer found family's establishment typical and not warranting exemption despite continued presence under removal order.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Immigration Officer acknowledged son's autism challenges but found autism services exist in Bangladesh; girls dependent and with no significant Canadian ties.
idea_list: availability of autism services in Bangladesh

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Immigration Officer rejected hardship claims about Bangladesh's poor employment and living conditions, viewing reintegration as ordinary consequence of removal.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Immigration Officer gave little or no positive weight to establishment, children's best interests, and country factors, refusing exemption under subsection 25(1).

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah's judicial review issue: whether the Decision was reasonable, focusing on establishment test and assessment of son's services in Bangladesh.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Parties agree standard of review is reasonableness; H&C exemptions are exceptional and discretionary, deserving deference.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah argues Immigration Officer wrongly applied an 'exceptional establishment' test, citing several cases against this standard.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds no impermissible exceptionality test; 'typical level of establishment' used descriptively and consistent with legal standards.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah contends Immigration Officer failed to assess whether establishment factors warranted humanitarian relief, lacking transparency.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court rejects claim of constrained analysis; finds Immigration Officer assessed establishment factors appropriately given limited evidence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds Immigration Officer considered broader H&C factors and hardship; no reason to disturb typical establishment conclusion.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah argues Immigration Officer improperly turned his education and mobility into a negative factor against exemption.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court disagrees; statement about education and mobility relates to country conditions, not establishment, and is not negative.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Immigration Officer acknowledged son's care needs but found specialized autism support services available in Bangladesh.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah concedes services exist in Bangladesh but argues they are inferior and availability was not properly assessed by Immigration Officer.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Minister argues best interests of children are not determinative and onus is on applicant to prove basis for positive discretion.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Immigration Officer detailed SWAC school services for autistic children, including individualized instruction and professional staff.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah argues Immigration Officer erred by assuming availability of limited enrolment services and unclear affordability at SWAC.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds Immigration Officer cannot assess accessibility or affordability issues not raised; Mr. Shah did not assert these concerns.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Immigration Officer reviewed UNICEF report showing governmental and NGO efforts to aid children with ASD in Bangladesh.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Shah argues Immigration Officer ignored UNICEF report's contrary evidence about discrimination and inadequate funding for disabled children.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court rejects Mr. Shah's assertions; presumes Immigration Officer reviewed evidence and Mr. Shah failed to prove son's best interests compromised.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court notes desirability of Canada or better services alone insufficient to grant H&C application.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds Immigration Officer's finding of available autism services in Bangladesh reasonable; no fundamental misapprehension of evidence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court decides to dismiss the application for judicial review.
